entities.name: Cleomenes the Cynic
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Cleomenes the Cynic, a Greek philosopher flourishing in the late 4th century BCE, served as a crucial conduit for Cynic thought following the foundational figures of Diogenes of Sinope and Crates of Thebes. Though his own writings are lost, his pedagogical role in transmitting the radical asceticism and ethical independence of Cynicism to the next generation, notably through his students Timarchus of Alexandria and Echecles of Ephesus, solidified his significance in the intellectual lineage of the school. His death around 300 BCE marks him as a transitional figure between the early, more direct Cynicism and its later, more diffuse influence across the Hellenistic world.

Emerging from the philosophical milieu of Athens, Cleomenes was a direct student of Crates of Thebes, who himself was a disciple of Diogenes of Sinope. This direct intellectual lineage placed Cleomenes firmly within the core tradition of Cynicism, emphasizing autarky (self-sufficiency), apatheia (freedom from disturbance), and parrhesia (frankness of speech). While no specific doctrines or major works are attributed to Cleomenes directly, his primary contribution lay in the oral transmission of Cynic principles. He is credited with teaching Timarchus of Alexandria and Echecles of Ephesus, thereby extending the geographical and chronological reach of Cynic philosophy beyond its Athenian origins.
